hints: Start by tracing the journey of a light-excited electron in each route - does it come back to where it started or does it end up somewhere new?
Think about how many photosystems are needed to keep that journey going, and where replacement electrons would have to come from if they do not return.
Now link each route to its products - which route can make both ATP and reducing power for the Calvin cycle, and which can only make ATP?
walkthrough:
Picture the electron route**
Think of non-cyclic flow as a one-way journey. Electrons excited in PSII pass along carriers to PSI, then to NADP. They are lost from the chlorophyll and must be replaced. In cyclic flow it is a loop. Electrons excited in PSI pass through electron carriers including cytochrome b6f and back to PSI, so no replacement is needed.

Add photosystems and water**
Because non-cyclic flow loses electrons, it needs two photosystems working together and a supply of electrons from splitting water by photolysis, which releases oxygen as a by-product. Cyclic flow recycles its own electrons, so it needs PSI only, no photolysis and no oxygen.

Link to ATP and reduced NADP**
Both routes pump protons to make ATP by photophosphorylation. Only non-cyclic flow ends with electrons reducing NADP to reduced NADP, using NADP reductase. So pick any three paired differences and state cyclic vs non-cyclic clearly to earn all 3 marks.

Final answer: Cyclic uses photosystem I only, non-cyclic uses photosystems I and II; in cyclic electrons return to PSI/P700, in non-cyclic they do not; cyclic makes ATP only, non-cyclic makes ATP and reduced NADP; non-cyclic involves photolysis of water and release of oxygen, cyclic does not.

hints: Look at the first gap - a one-carbon inorganic molecule joins the five-carbon RuBP to start the cycle. What gas enters the leaf for photosynthesis?
The joining of that gas to RuBP needs a very abundant chloroplast enzyme whose name starts with R. Recall the carboxylase involved in fixation.
To turn GP into triose phosphate needs energy from ATP plus hydrogen and electrons from a reduced coenzyme made in the light-dependent stage.
For the last gap, think of what the plant builds from triose phosphate that is not recycled - from sugars and storage carbohydrate to lipids and proteins.
walkthrough:
Carbon fixation**
The Calvin cycle starts when a molecule of carbon dioxide combines with ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP. This carboxylation is catalysed by the enzyme Rubisco. The unstable six-carbon compound at once splits into two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate, GP.

Reduction to triose phosphate**
GP is then reduced to triose phosphate, TP. That needs ATP for energy and NADPH, the reduced NADP from non-cyclic photophosphorylation, to supply hydrogen and electrons.

Fate of triose phosphate**
Most TP is recycled with ATP to regenerate RuBP to keep the cycle turning. Some TP leaves the cycle to make useful organic products such as glucose, starch, cellulose, lipids or amino acids and proteins.
Final answer: carbon dioxide; Rubisco; NADPH / reduced NADP; glucose / hexose / starch / cellulose / glycerol / fatty acids / lipids / amino acids / proteins.
